query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating actively learned moment tensor potentials with an analytical free-energy model that explicitly retains vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling can reliably compute fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties at a fraction of the cost of explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental and binary systems at conditions near their fusion (melting) points, with the potential extension to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
generation.intervention: Replace the expensive explicit molecular-dynamics free-energy evaluation by training moment tensor potentials through an active learning scheme (as demonstrated in refractory MPEA studies) and coupling these potentials to an analytical free-energy approximation that preserves critical entropy contributions.
generation.conditions: This method is to be applied under high-temperature conditions (~0.9–1.1 of the melting temperature) in systems ranging from elemental and binary alloys up to multicomponent high-entropy systems where free energy differences between solid and fluid states are crucial.
generation.structural_mediator: Machine-learned moment tensor potentials that capture local bonding, anharmonic vibrational behavior, and the effects of electron–vibration interactions.
generation.mechanism: The moment tensor potentials emulate the ab initio potential energy surface with high fidelity while offering a dramatic reduction in computational cost. Coupling these with an analytical model ensures that essential entropy contributions are not lost, thus maintaining accuracy in the computed free energies for both phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: The fusion free energies and related thermodynamic observables will be obtained with accuracy comparable to explicit ab initio MD (within ~5% error) but with computational speeds improved by at least one order of magnitude relative to TOR-TILD and ab initio MD.
generation.baseline: Traditional explicit ab initio molecular dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD approaches that compute free energies directly.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to work in systems that range from elemental and binary alloys to complex multicomponent high-entropy alloys, particularly near the phase transition temperature. Beyond these composition or temperature ranges, additional validation would be required.
generation.uncertainty: While active learning of moment tensor potentials has shown promise in optimizing relevant mechanical properties and free energies in simpler systems, its quantitative accuracy for fusion properties across diverse and multicomponent systems has not been fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Select benchmark systems (e.g., a well-characterized binary alloy and a representative multicomponent high-entropy alloy) with documented ab initio MD free energies and transition temperatures. Use the hybrid active learning moment tensor potential plus analytical model to compute the solid and fluid phase free energies, then compare the computed phase-transition observables (free energies, vibrational entropy contributions, melting temperatures) to those obtained from explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD methods.
measurements: Fusion free energies for both solid and liquid phases
Relative computational time and resource usage
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hybrid approach yields discrepancies exceeding approximately 5% in free energy or phase-transition temperatures, or if the computational speed improvement is less than 10x compared to explicit ab initio MD/TOR-TILD for the benchmark systems, the hypothesis will be falsified.

## Abstract
While first-principles methods have been successfully applied to characterize individual properties of multi-principal element alloys (MPEA), their use in searching for optimal trade-offs between competing properties is hampered by high computational demands. In this work, we present a framework to explore Pareto-optimal compositions by integrating advanced ab initio-based techniques into a Bayesian multi-objective optimization workflow, complemented by a simple analytical model providing straightforward analysis of trends. We benchmark the framework by applying it to solid solution strengthening and ductility of refractory MPEAs, with the parameters of the strengthening and ductility models being efficiently computed using a combination of the coherent-potential approximation method, accounting for finite-temperature effects, and actively-learned moment-tensor potentials parameterized with ab initio data. ## Abstract
AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys composed of five or more primary elements in equal or nearly equal proportions of atoms. In the present study, the thermophysical properties of the CoCrFeNiCu high entropy alloy (HEA) were investigated by a molecular dynamics (MD) method at nanoscale. The effects of the content of individual elements on lattice thermal conductivity kp were revealed, and the results suggested that adjusting the atomic content can be a way to control the lattice thermal conductivity of HEAs. The effects of temperature on kp were investigated quantitively, and a power-law relationship of kp with T−0.419 was suggested, which agrees with previous findings. The effects of temperature and the content of individual elements on volumetric specific heat capacity Cv were also studied: as the temperature increases, the Cv of all HEAs slightly decreases and then increases. The effects of atomic content on Cv varied with the comprising elements.
